title: 1883 eruption of Krakatoa
description: Volcanic eruption in the Sunda Strait
wiki_lead:
Between 19 May and 21 October 1883, the volcanic island of Krakatoa (located in the Sunda Strait, then part of the Dutch East Indies—modern-day Indonesia) began erupting, lasting more than five months. On 27 August, the island had its most significant eruption, which destroyed over 70% of the island and its surrounding archipelago, the island collapsing into a caldera. The eruption of 27 August had an estimated volcanic explosivity index of 6, and is one of the deadliest and most destructive volcanic events in recorded history; the third explosion of that day, that occurred at 10:02 a.m., remains the loudest-known sound in history.
The explosion was heard 3,110 kilometres (1,930 mi) away in Perth, Western Australia, and Rodrigues near Mauritius, 4,800 kilometres (3,000 mi) away. The acoustic pressure wave circled the globe more than three times. At least 36,417 deaths are attributed to the eruption and the tsunamis it created. Significant additional effects were felt worldwide in the days and weeks after the volcano's eruption. Additional seismic activity was reported until February 1884, but any reports after October 1883 were dismissed by Rogier Verbeek's subsequent investigation into the eruption.

Eruption


Early phase

In the years before the 1883 eruption, seismic activity around the Krakatoa volcano was intense, with earthquakes felt as far away as the Australian Northern Territory, one of which, in 1880, damaged a lighthouse. Strombolian activity began on 20 May 1883, and steam venting began to occur regularly from Perboewatan, the northernmost of the island's three cones. Eruptions of ash reached an estimated altitude of 6 kilometres (20,000 ft), and explosions could be heard in Batavia (Jakarta) 160 km (100 mi) away, rattling windows and doors. Dust fell 480 km (300 mi) away. An excursion party sent to the island on 26 May reported that the islands were covered with a fine white dust, with explosions coming from Perboewatan every five to ten minutes. Although by this time the eruptions were calming down, some of the explosions were still very energetic, hurling pumice opposite the direction of the wind. A large crater approximately 900 metres (3,000 ft) in diameter formed, with a cavity from which issued plumes of steam. The eruptions soon quietened after the initial violence.
Around 16 June, there were loud explosions and a thick black cloud covered the islands for five days. The eruptions started gaining strength again on 19 June. On 24 June, a prevailing east wind cleared the cloud, and two ash columns could be seen issuing from Krakatau. It was also noticed that the summit cone of Perboewatan was gone, which an extensive report of a few years later attributes it to having been blown away. The seat of the eruption is believed to have been a new vent or vents that formed on that day, between Perboewatan and Danan. grok_lead: The 1883 eruption of Krakatoa was a cataclysmic volcanic event that occurred between August 26 and 27 on the island of Krakatoa (also known as Krakatau) in Indonesia's Sunda Strait, between the islands of Java and Sumatra, culminating in the partial destruction of the volcano and the generation of devastating tsunamis that killed more than 36,000 people, making it one of the deadliest eruptions in recorded history. The eruption registered a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 6, ejecting over 20 cubic kilometers of tephra and debris into the atmosphere, with pyroclastic flows and explosions that obliterated more than two-thirds of the 18-square-mile island. Preceded by minor seismic activity and steam emissions starting in May 1883, the main explosive phase began on August 26 with a series of increasingly violent blasts, including the largest at 10:02 a.m. on August 27, which produced a pressure wave equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT that circled the globe up to seven times over five days and was heard up to 3,000 miles (4,800 km) away in locations such as Perth, Australia, and Rodrigues Island near Mauritius, marking it as the loudest sound in recorded human history. The collapse of the volcano's chambers triggered tsunami s reaching heights of 135 feet (41 meters) in some areas, which inundated coastal villages across Java and Sumatra, destroying 165 settlements and causing the vast majority of fatalities through drowning and structural collapse. Pyroclastic surges also raced across the sea at speeds over 60 mph (100 km/h), incinerating everything in their path and contributing to additional deaths estimated at around 4,000. The eruption's global repercussions were profound, as fine ash and sulfur aerosols propelled into the stratosphereâreaching heights of 50 miles (80 km)âcircumnavigated the Earth multiple times, leading to vivid red sunsets observable worldwide for years and a temporary global cooling of about 0.9Â°F (0.5Â°C) that disrupted weather patterns and agriculture for up to three years. These atmospheric effects blanketed an area of 300,000 square miles (777,000 square km) in ash and caused optical phenomena like blue moons and vivid red sunsetsâincluding in Connecticut, where the red skies were mistaken for a local fireâdue to the scattering of sunlight by sub-micron particles. Scientifically, the event was the first major eruption extensively documented with telegraphic reports, barographs, and ship logs, providing invaluable data on volcanic propagation, tsunami dynamics, and climate forcing that influenced modern volcanology and disaster preparedness.
